strengths: The core idea is compelling: combining an S5-based encoder with a functional basis decoder (FBD) that emits a continuous forecast, sampled at any spacing Δ, is a clean solution to sampling-rate invariance and variable-horizon forecasting that most TSFMs handle with patching or autoregression hacks.

The empirical results are strong: FlowState-9.1M tops both GIFT-ZS and Chronos-ZS leaderboards while being ~4–50x smaller than competing models, and the 2.6M variant remains competitive, supporting the efficiency claim.

The paper shows commendable care regarding data contamination: it identifies test-data leakage in prior leaderboards (e.g., TiRex pretraining on GIFT-Eval tasks), constructs a decontaminated GIFT-ZS subset, evaluates leakage-free variants on Chronos-ZS, and transparently flags leakage status in Table 3. This honesty strengthens the credibility of the SOTA claims.

The ablation study (Table 4) directly tests each claimed component: removing time-scale adjustment causes a large degradation (MASE 0.733→0.808), parallel predictions and CPM/MPI also contribute measurably, and decoder basis variants are compared.

The controlled subsampling experiment on Loop Seattle (5–65 min intervals) provides direct, targeted evidence for the central sampling-rate-invariance claim, showing baselines only close the gap at commonly pretrained frequencies (15T/30T/60T).
The causal running-statistics normalization (Eqs. 8–10) is a well-motivated fix to RevIN's train/test leakage under the parallel-forecast training scheme.
weaknesses: The probabilistic forecasting mechanism is never described. Benchmarks are scored with WQL/CRPS (quantile metrics), and the paper claims MPI 'propagates uncertainty,' yet the FBD as formalized (Eqs. 3–5) produces only a point forecast from the final encoder output. How quantiles are generated is unexplained, which undermines understanding of a headline result.

Notation and equations contain errors: Eq. 1 mixes conventions (B̄ acting on x^{l-1} vs. x_t); the matrix dimension listing (B̄ ∈ R^{c×P} for a state update, plus undefined 'm and n') is inconsistent; Eq. 9 computes variance as cumsum((μ_{r,t} − x)^2)/t, which is not the running variance (should be centered on deviations from μ_{r,t}), and no numerical stability term is mentioned.

The s_Δ selection at evaluation time is a hand-tuned heuristic based on dataset seasonality (base seasonality 24). Baselines do not receive comparable per-dataset tuning, so the headline benchmark comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples; sensitivity of results to this heuristic is not analyzed.

Statistical rigor is lacking: results are single-run geometric means with no confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed variance, despite differences between FlowState and TiRex being small in places (e.g., MASE 0.719 vs. 0.733).

The full GIFT-Eval results (Table 3) show FlowState(T) still behind TiRex (0.728 vs. 0.724), and the paper itself admits the full benchmark has 'not yet been extensively analyzed' — the strongest SOTA claims rest on the modified subset benchmark.

The robustness experiment covers only one dataset (Loop Seattle), one target length (480), and apparently one seed; generalization of the sampling-rate conclusion beyond traffic-like data is not established.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or model release is mentioned, and pretraining details (data volumes, compute, optimization schedule, number of epochs, tokenizer/scaling of multivariate channels) are sparse or absent.

There is no limitations section; claims such as avoiding 'training data across all possible sampling rates' are somewhat overstated given the s_Δ heuristic and that pretraining augmentation still spans frequencies.

The FBD's capacity limits (a single coefficient vector per forecast via Legendre polynomials) and why Fourier/Half-Legendre perform nearly identically deserve deeper analysis; the contribution is more an engineering recombination of known ideas (S5, HiPPO-style decoding, CPM/MPI) than a conceptual advance, though the empirical outcome is genuinely useful.

strengths: Strong empirical results: FlowState-9.1M achieves the best MASE/CRPS on the GIFT-ZS subset and best MASE/WQL on Chronos-ZS, outperforming models up to ~50x larger (TiRex 35M, TimesFM-2.0 500M); leaderboard-verifiable rather than self-constructed comparisons.

Careful treatment of data contamination: the paper identifies overlap between the Chronos pretraining corpus and GIFT-Eval, constructs the GIFT-ZS subset (79/97 tasks), and explicitly flags which FlowState variants and baselines have test-data leakage (Table 3 TDL column). This is more rigorous than much of the TSFM literature.

The functional basis decoder is a genuinely interesting idea: interpreting the encoder output as coefficients of a continuous basis so that the forecast can be sampled at arbitrary resolution is a clean mechanism for horizon/resolution flexibility, and the paper correctly notes it is encoder-agnostic.
Useful technical component: the causal reformulation of RevIN (running mean/variance) is necessary for parallel forecasting to avoid leakage, and the derivation is clear.

Ablations (Table 4) cover the main components (time-scale adjustment, parallel predictions, basis choice, CPM/MPI), and the paper honestly reports that the CPM advantage largely disappears when retraining with a longer base target, which increases trust.
Well-written and well-organized; Figures 1 and 2 effectively communicate the architecture and the parallel-prediction training scheme.
weaknesses: The central 'sampling rate invariance' claim rests heavily on a known property of S5 (discretization-time rescaling, Smith et al. 2023). The genuine novelty is the FBD plus the s∆ scaling, yet the only direct evidence for robustness to unseen sampling rates is a single controlled experiment on a single dataset (Loop Seattle, Figure 3). A claim this central needs broader empirical support (multiple datasets, ablation of s∆ selection, comparison against baselines given the same oracle sampling-rate information).

The seasonality-based heuristic for choosing s∆ at evaluation time (s∆ = Base Seasonality / Seasonality) effectively gives the model per-dataset metadata that baselines do not receive. This makes the 'inherently adapts to input scale' framing somewhat overstated: an oracle-like dataset-specific parameter is being injected, and the sensitivity to this choice is not analyzed.

The probabilistic forecasting mechanism is never explained. Both benchmarks score WQL/CRPS, which requires quantile forecasts, but the paper does not describe how quantiles are produced from a continuous functional-basis output (quantile heads? output dimension per coefficient? sampling-based?). This is a material soundness gap for the headline results.

Notational and dimensional ambiguities in the method section: the S5 matrices are inconsistently dimensioned across layers (B ∈ R^{c×P} but C ∈ R^{P×H} with m, n introduced but never used), and it is unclear how a single coefficient vector o^N_L (Eq. 3) yields multivariate forecasts and multiple quantiles.

Missing details needed for reproducibility: pretraining corpus sizes, training hyperparameters, number of basis functions, how L_eff/T_eff interact with the fixed 2048/24 effective lengths per task, and no mention of code or model release. As written, others cannot reliably rebuild or build on FlowState.

Some claims exceed the evidence: 'reduced data requirements' is asserted in the abstract but never tested (no data-scaling experiments); 'improved efficiency' is claimed via the parallel-forecast training scheme but no wall-clock or FLOP comparisons to baselines are reported.

The gains, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms (e.g., MASE 0.719 vs 0.733 for TiRex on GIFT-ZS), and the 2.6M variant is roughly on par with TiRex rather than clearly better; the efficiency story would need to carry more weight, but it is under-supported (see above).

The temporal-scaling evaluation protocol (effective lengths L_eff, T_eff, base target of 24) is nonstandard and only applies to FlowState; it is plausible but introduces evaluation choices that could favor the proposed method and are not validated against an alternative protocol.

strengths: Strong empirical results: FlowState achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on GIFT-ZS and Chronos-ZS with only 2.6M–9.1M parameters, outperforming models up to ~192× larger (e.g., TiRex at 35M, TimesFM-2.0 at 500M), which is a meaningful efficiency result.

The functional basis decoder (FBD) is a genuinely interesting and well-motivated idea: connecting the decoder to HiPPO-style coefficient representations yields a continuous forecast that can be sampled at arbitrary resolutions, and the component is modular enough to combine with other encoders.

The paper handles data leakage with unusual care: it identifies that TiRex and other leaderboard models pretrain on GIFT-Eval evaluation data, constructs a clean GIFT-ZS subset (79/97 tasks), trains FlowState(T) without Chronos data for the Chronos-ZS comparison, and transparently reports a Test Data Leakage column in Table 3. This materially strengthens the credibility of the SOTA claims.

The causal RevIN variant is a necessary and correct observation — standard RevIN leaks future context statistics into per-prefix predictions, which would invalidate the parallel-forecast training scheme; the running-statistics fix is sensible.

Ablations (Table 4) isolate the contributions of the time-scale adjustment, parallel predictions, basis choice, and CPM/MPI, and the controlled subsampling experiment on Loop Seattle provides direct evidence for the sampling-rate robustness claim on frequencies unseen during pretraining.
weaknesses: The mechanism for producing probabilistic forecasts is never described, yet WQL/CRPS are headline metrics. The FBD as formalized (Eqs. 3–5) produces a deterministic point forecast; how quantiles are generated (a quantile head? sampling? ensembling?) is unspecified, which makes the probabilistic results hard to interpret and reproduce.

Reproducibility gaps: key hyperparameters (number of S5 layers N, state/output dimensions, training details, number of pretraining tokens, quantile setup), the exact construction of the scale factor s_Δ per dataset (how seasonality is detected for truly unseen datasets), and code/data release plans are not provided. As written, the model cannot be reproduced from the manuscript.

The sampling-rate robustness evidence is thin relative to the central claim: it rests on a single dataset (Loop Seattle), a single metric (MAE), and one model size. The claim of 'adapting online to varying input sampling rates' in the abstract is only indirectly supported; a demonstration where s_Δ is mis-specified or the sampling rate shifts mid-series would be needed to substantiate online adaptation.

The evaluation protocol is partly self-defined: GIFT-ZS is the authors' own subset of GIFT-Eval, and temporal scaling requires dataset-specific seasonality information at evaluation time. While leakage handling is commendable, results on a custom subset complicate direct comparability with leaderboard numbers, and the sensitivity of results to the GIFT-ZS task selection is not analyzed.

Some ablation results partially undercut the narrative: 'No CPM training, longer target' achieves better MASE (0.731 vs 0.733) than the full model, suggesting MPI mainly helps probabilistic metrics; this nuance deserves more discussion.

Presentation issues: dimension notation in the S5 equations is inconsistent (matrices B, C, D are typed with dimensions involving c, P, H while the text refers to undefined sizes m and n), and parts of the experimental setup are compressed to the point of ambiguity.

Baseline comparisons on Chronos-ZS and the full GIFT-Eval rely heavily on leaderboard-reported numbers rather than fully controlled re-evaluations, and the sampling-rate experiment lacks baselines that also receive a comparable scale factor, so the margin partly reflects protocol asymmetry.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem: existing TSFMs are inflexible w.r.t. sampling rate, context/target length, and require large parameter counts; FlowState addresses all three within a coherent design.

Novel functional basis decoder (FBD) that treats SSM encoder outputs as coefficients of a continuous basis (Legendre polynomials), enabling forecasts sampleable at any rate — a genuinely new and architecturally clean mechanism for sampling-rate equivariance, and modular enough to pair with other encoders.

The paper provides both a theoretical treatment (single-layer ZOH mismatch bound with a Lipschitz/extension argument to multiple layers in Appendix B) and empirical validation of equivariance (ETT1h-context → ETT1m-target predictions; encoding-correlation analysis in Fig. 8), rather than relying on claims alone.

Strong empirical results: SOTA MASE (0.701) and CRPS (0.487) on the full GIFT-Eval benchmark with only 18.6M parameters, roughly 10x smaller than TimesFM-2.5; a 3M variant is still competitive. Additional standard-benchmark results (Table 3) support generality.

The controlled resampling experiment on ETT1m (Fig. 4) directly demonstrates the headline claim: consistent advantages at unseen sampling intervals (15–135 min) where baselines only close the gap at frequencies likely seen during pretraining.

Comprehensive ablation study (Table 2) with seed-based variance estimates for the baseline, covering core components, encoder/decoder choices, training details, and inference-time variants (truncating basis functions), with sensible interpretations of each result.

Practical training contributions: parallel forecasts over increasing context lengths plus the necessary causal RevIN variant are well-motivated, shown to matter in ablations, and presented as architecture-agnostic techniques.

Honest limitations section (heuristic scale-factor selection, univariate-only design) with concrete analysis of the automatic scale-factor selection fallback (D.2.2) and scale-factor sensitivity (Fig. 9), plus training details sufficient to aid reproduction.
weaknesses: The theoretical equivariance guarantee is proven only for a single SSM layer under idealized assumptions (Lipschitz input, exponential stability, bounded pointwise maps); the multi-layer extension is a heuristic recursion argument, so the formal claim supporting the central property is weaker than the framing in the main text suggests.

The headline GIFT-Eval comparison (Table 1) relies on leaderboard numbers for baselines rather than retraining them under the same pretraining corpus; differences in pretraining data/augmentation across models confound the attribution of the gains to the architecture, even though the data mixes (GIFT-Eval-Pretrain + Chronos + CauKer synthetic) largely overlap with competitors'.

Scale-factor selection in the main experiments requires external seasonality knowledge (dataset-level mapping from sampling rate and domain, Algorithm 1, plus a hand-picked exception for 'bizitobs_l2c'); while the automatic fallback is evaluated, it costs noticeable performance (0.725 → 0.746 MASE), so the practical deployment story for truly unseen datasets is not fully resolved.

Absolute improvements over the strongest baseline are modest (0.705 → 0.701 MASE, identical CRPS for TiRex at 0.488/0.487), and main results are single-seed; the parameter-efficiency argument is compelling but the accuracy gains themselves are within plausible run-to-run variation.

FlowState is univariate-only and processes channels independently; multi-variate/covariate support is deferred to future work, which limits applicability relative to several competing TSFMs that handle these natively.
No explicit statement of code or model release, which limits reproducibility of a foundation-model contribution despite detailed hyperparameter tables.

Some novelty overlaps with prior work — sampling-rate adjustment of SSMs via Δ is known (Smith et al., 2023), and multi-context training has antecedents — so the paper's distinct contribution rests mainly on the FBD plus the equivariance framing; the paper handles this reasonably but could delineate more sharply.

strengths: The core architectural idea is clean and well-motivated: pairing an S5-style SSM encoder (which is naturally continuous-time) with a functional basis decoder that emits a continuous forecast sampled at an arbitrary rate is a sensible route to sampling-rate-equivariant forecasting, and the FBD is presented as a reusable component rather than being entangled with the rest of the model.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough for this area: SOTA-level GIFT-Eval results with a much smaller parameter count (FlowState-10.6M/18.6M vs. TimesFM-2.5 at 200M), supplementary results on standard benchmarks (Table 3), a controlled resampling experiment on ETT1m across 15–135 minute intervals showing robustness at unseen frequencies (Figure 4), and a fairly comprehensive ablation table covering core components, encoder/decoder variants, and training choices, with seed variance reported for the ablation baseline.

The parallel-forecast training scheme is a simple but effective contribution: exploiting SSM parallelism to produce ~4076 forecasts per sample during pretraining improves both efficiency and robustness to varying context lengths, and the ablation (0.725 → 0.774 MASE without it) supports the claim. The accompanying causal RevIN fix is a correct and useful observation, since standard RevIN would leak future statistics in this setup.

Reproducibility is above average: pretraining corpora are enumerated in the appendix, training hyperparameters and model sizes are given, the seasonality heuristic is spelled out as pseudocode, an automatic scale-factor variant and a sensitivity analysis (Figure 9) are included, and the limitations section honestly identifies the heuristic scale selection, univariate-only processing, and lack of covariate support.

The equivariance analysis in Appendix B is a genuine attempt at formal grounding, including a multi-layer recursion argument, and is complemented by an empirical encoding-similarity experiment (Figure 8) with an appropriate misalignment control.
weaknesses: The headline 'sampling-rate equivariance' claim is weaker than advertised in practice. The formal guarantee is only first-order approximate, proven strictly for a single SSM layer with exponential stability and Lipschitz assumptions (the multi-layer case is deferred to a heuristic recursion), and at inference time the model depends on a per-dataset scale factor sΔ derived from externally supplied seasonality/domain knowledge (Algorithm 1, including a hand-coded exception for one dataset). Baselines do not receive comparable per-dataset tuning, so part of the GIFT-Eval advantage may come from this dataset-specific prior rather than from architectural superiority. The automatic variant degrades notably (0.725 → 0.746 MASE), and Figure 9 shows real sensitivity to misaligned factors.

The novelty is more incremental than the framing suggests. The encoder is essentially S5 with an output gate, and rate adaptation of SSMs via adjusting Δ is known (Smith et al., 2023); the paper itself notes this. The central novelty reduces to (i) scaling Δ at inference, (ii) the functional-basis decoder, and (iii) the parallel-forecast training scheme. All three are reasonable, but the FBD's benefit over a fixed decoder (0.725 → 0.754) is moderate, and the top-line GIFT-Eval margin over TimesFM-2.5 is small (0.701 vs. 0.705 MASE) given the extra per-dataset scale information FlowState consumes.

The model does not natively handle multivariate data or covariates, processing channels independently in univariate mode. For a 'foundation model' positioned against Chronos-2 and TiRex (which do support multivariate/covariate settings), this is a substantial capability gap that limits the significance of the contribution, even if the authors flag it as a deliberate simplification.

Some experimental reporting choices are not fully transparent or favorable: Figure 4 normalizes MAE 'vs. FlowState as baseline', which makes cross-model comparison harder to interpret than reporting raw or seasonally-naive-normalized errors; Table 1 compares against 'strongest public zero-shot models ... who offer code for verification', excluding possibly strong leaderboard entries; and main experiments were run once (seed 0) with variance estimated only for the 3M ablation baseline.

Presentation has gaps that impede verification: dimensions in Section 3.1 are inconsistent (A ∈ R^{P×P} but B ∈ R^{c×P}, with 'm and n' undefined where 'P and H' seem intended), the FBD formalization (Eqs. 4–6) is loose (the interval [a,b], the forecast horizon, and how quantiles are produced by a single continuous function are not precisely specified), and the claim that one continuous forecast carries per-timestep quantile information deserves more explanation.

The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions (Lipschitz input, exponentially stable A with the specific Re(λ) = -exp(θ) parameterization) whose tightness in the trained model is unquantified; the constant C in Eq. 47 involves worst-case Lipschitz constants that could be very large, so the bound is more of a qualitative argument than a quantitative guarantee.

strengths: The central contribution is well-motivated and genuinely novel: the functional basis decoder (FBD) that interprets SSM outputs as coefficients of a continuous functional basis is a clean mechanism for continuous-time forecasting, and the combination with a ZOH-discretized SSM yields approximate sampling-rate equivariance, which no competing TSFM currently offers.

Strong empirical results: FlowState-18.6M achieves the best MASE (0.701) and CRPS (0.487) on the widely used GIFT-Eval benchmark while being roughly an order of magnitude smaller than TimesFM-2.5 (200M), TiRex (35M), Chronos-2 (120M), and Toto (151M). The parameter efficiency claim is well supported.

The controlled unseen-sampling-rate experiment (ETT1m resampled to 15–135 minute intervals) directly targets the paper's core claim and shows consistent advantages over TiRex, TimesFM-2.5, and Chronos-2-Synth, particularly at uncommon sampling frequencies, which is exactly where non-equivariant models should struggle.

The paper includes a formal analysis of the equivariance property (Appendix B), with a clearly stated single-layer ZOH-mismatch bound under explicit assumptions (input Lipschitz continuity, exponential stability), a discussion of multi-layer extension via a recursion argument, and empirical validation of encoder invariance via cosine-similarity correlation matrices (Figure 8). The theory is honest about its scope rather than overclaiming.

Comprehensive and well-organized ablations (Table 2) that isolate the encoder, decoder, core components, and training details, with error estimates from three seeds for the baseline. The qualitative analysis of the fixed-decoder ablation (Appendix A.2) is a nice addition that explains *why* the degradation is only moderate.
The causal RevIN contribution is well-argued: it identifies a subtle information leakage in standard RevIN when combined with parallel forecasts, which is independently useful.

Reproducibility is good: pretraining data are enumerated in detail (Appendix C), hyperparameters are fully specified (Tables 7–8), the scale-factor selection procedure is given as pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and an automatic scale-factor variant plus sensitivity analysis (Figure 9, Appendix D.2) is included.
Limitations are discussed candidly (heuristic scale-factor selection, univariate-only processing), and the ablations reinforce rather than undermine the central claims.
weaknesses: The formal equivariance guarantee is only proven for a single SSM layer; the multi-layer extension relies on an informal recursion with assumed uniform Lipschitz/stability constants. This is acceptable for an architecture paper, but the headline 'sampling-rate equivariant' claim is technically approximate and unproven for the actual model.

The scale factor s_∆ is computed using dataset-level metadata (domain labels and a hand-crafted seasonality mapping, Algorithm 1), which weakens the 'generalizes to unseen sampling rates without retraining' narrative — the model still requires per-dataset temporal scaling input, and the automatic alternative degrades MASE from 0.725 to 0.746. Practical deployment in truly unknown-rate settings remains unresolved.

The main GIFT-Eval results appear to be single runs (seed 0, 'experiments were executed once'), with seed variance only estimated for the 3M/2k ablation baseline; the margins over TimesFM-2.5 (0.701 vs 0.705 MASE) are small enough that run-to-run variance at the 10.6M/18.6M scale would be informative.

The equivariance experiment (Figure 2) and the robustness study (Figure 4) are restricted to a single dataset family (ETT); broader evidence across domains would strengthen the generality of the sampling-rate claim.
Figure 4 normalizes MAE 'vs. FlowState as baseline,' which makes the magnitude of baselines' degradation hard to assess from the plot alone; a table with absolute errors would be clearer.

The parallel-forecast training scheme and ZOH-adjustment of ∆ are related to existing ideas (contiguous patch masking / MPI from TiRex, sampling-rate adjustment in S5/Smith et al. 2023); the paper does position this, but the FBD's novelty relative to prior coefficient-based decoders (e.g., HiPPO/Legendre projections) could be delineated more explicitly.
No explicit statement about code or model-weight release, which limits reproducibility of pretraining despite the detailed documentation.
